ancient-near-east.title: The Queen of the Night
ancient-near-east.meta: Babylonia, about 1800–1750 BCE · fired clay, about 50 cm tall · British Museum
paras: A winged goddess, naked but for a horned crown, stands on two lions between two great owls. Her feet are the talons of a bird of prey, and in each hand she holds the rod and ring, the emblems of divine justice. She was once painted: red body, black wings and owls, a crown picked out in colour.

No one is sure who she is: Ishtar, goddess of love and war; her sister Ereshkigal, queen of the dead; or a demon of the night. She was made in the age that wrote down the Old Babylonian Gilgamesh and the descent of the goddess into the underworld, and she has the look of both.

anglo-saxon.title: The Sutton Hoo Helmet
anglo-saxon.meta: East Anglia, early 7th century · iron and tinned bronze · shown here in a modern replica
paras: In 1939 a mound at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk was found to hold the ghost of a ship, ninety feet long, with a king’s treasure in its burial chamber: gold buckles, a sword, silver from Byzantium, and this helmet, crushed into hundreds of pieces. Rebuilt, it shows a face of metal whose eyebrows end in boars’ heads and whose nose and brows together make a bird in flight.

The king was probably Rædwald of East Anglia, who died about 624. Beowulf opens with just such a funeral, Scyld Scefing laid in his ship with treasure heaped about him, and its warriors go into battle under boar-crested helmets.
anglo-saxon.credit: Photograph: Philip Halling, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

medieval.title: The Wilton Diptych
medieval.meta: England or France, about 1395–99 · tempera and gold on oak · National Gallery, London
paras: On this panel the Virgin holds out the Christ Child among eleven angels in a blaze of ultramarine, the most precious blue there was, ground from lapis lazuli. Every angel wears the badge of a white hart, the emblem of King Richard II, who kneels on the facing panel, and one holds up the banner of St George.

It was painted for Richard himself, the king of Chaucer and Gower and of the poet of Pearl, a few years before he lost his throne. Shakespeare would make him the hero of a tragedy two centuries later.

tudor-elizabethan.title: The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I
tudor-elizabethan.meta: England, about 1588 · oil on panel · one of three surviving versions
paras: Painted to celebrate the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588, it sets the Queen between two windows: on one side the English fireships drive at the Spanish fleet, on the other the Armada is wrecked in a storm. Her hand rests on a globe, over the Americas, and an imperial crown waits at her elbow. Pearls, emblems of her virginity, are everywhere.
This is the Queen to whom Spenser dedicated The Faerie Queene (1590), as Gloriana, and in whose reign Marlowe, Sidney, Raleigh and the young Shakespeare wrote.

metaphysical-cavalier.title: Charles I in Three Positions
metaphysical-cavalier.meta: Sir Anthony van Dyck, 1635–36 · oil on canvas · Royal Collection
paras: Van Dyck painted the King in profile, full face and three-quarter view so that the sculptor Bernini, in Rome, could carve a marble bust of a man he would never see. The bust was made, admired, and lost in the fire that destroyed Whitehall Palace in 1698. The painting survives.

Charles was the king of the Cavalier poets, Lovelace, Carew, Suckling and Herrick, and his execution in 1649 drew from Marvell the most famous lines ever written about him: “He nothing common did or mean / Upon that memorable scene.”

restoration-augustan.title: The City of London on Lord Mayor’s Day
restoration-augustan.meta: Canaletto, about 1747–48 · oil on canvas · Lobkowicz Collections, Prague
paras: Wren’s new St Paul’s rises over a London rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1666, its spires all new, while the Thames below is crowded with state barges carrying the Lord Mayor to Westminster. Canaletto painted it during his years in England.
This is the city of Dryden’s Annus Mirabilis, of Pope’s Dunciad and Gay’s Trivia, a poem on the art of walking its streets, and of the river that Pope called, in Windsor-Forest, “Old Father Thames”.

romantic.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
romantic.meta: Caspar David Friedrich, about 1818 · oil on canvas · Hamburger Kunsthalle
paras: A man stands with his back to us on a rocky summit, looking out over a sea of mist from which other peaks rise like islands. We see what he sees, but never his face.

It is the Romantic moment exactly. Wordsworth climbed Snowdon by night and came out above the clouds to find “a huge sea of mist” beneath the moon, the vision that crowns The Prelude; Shelley stood before Mont Blanc, and Byron’s Manfred on the Jungfrau.

victorian.title: The Lady of Shalott
victorian.meta: John William Waterhouse, 1888 · oil on canvas · Tate Britain
paras: Tennyson’s Lady has left her loom and broken the curse; she has written her name round the prow of a boat and drifts down to Camelot, singing, to her death. Two of the three candles have gone out. The tapestry she wove trails in the water.

“And down the river’s dim expanse / Like some bold seër in a trance … / Did she look to Camelot.” Waterhouse painted the moment from Part IV of the poem, half a century after Tennyson published it, and it became one of the best-loved pictures in England.

american.title: The Oxbow
american.meta: Thomas Cole, 1836 · oil on canvas · Metropolitan Museum of Art
paras: From the top of Mount Holyoke in Massachusetts a thunderstorm passes away over the wild forest on the left, while on the right the Connecticut River loops through farms and fields in sunlight. Cole, the founder of the Hudson River School, set wilderness and settlement side by side, and painted himself small at his easel in the foreground.
His close friend was the poet William Cullen Bryant, who wrote of these same forests in “Thanatopsis” and “A Forest Hymn”, and who spoke at Cole’s funeral.
american.credit: Image: Metropolitan Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

modern.title: We Are Making a New World
modern.meta: Paul Nash, 1918 · oil on canvas · Imperial War Museum, London
paras: Shattered stumps that were once a wood stand in a churned waste of mud and shell holes, and a pale sun rises over them as if nothing had happened. Nash had served at Ypres; the bitter title is his own.
This is the landscape of Owen, Sassoon and Rosenberg, of “What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?”, and of the old world that modern poetry would try to make new.

turkish-ottoman.title: Istanbul from the Golden Horn
turkish-ottoman.meta: The Süleymaniye Mosque · Mimar Sinan, 1550–57 · photographed from the water
paras: Above the blue water of the Golden Horn rises the Süleymaniye, the mosque that the architect Sinan built for Süleyman the Magnificent on the city’s third hill, its great dome and four minarets set over the harbour where the ferries still cross between Europe and Asia.

For four centuries Istanbul was the capital of Ottoman poetry. Süleyman himself wrote verse under the pen name Muhibbi, and Bâkî, the sultan of poets, lies buried here; Nedîm sang the city’s gardens and pleasures, and opened a famous poem: “This city of Istanbul, beyond compare and beyond price.”
turkish-ottoman.credit: Photograph: Canercangul, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

arabic-persian.title: The Court of Gayumars
arabic-persian.meta: Sultan Muhammad, about 1522–25 · from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp
paras: Ferdowsi’s Shahnama, finished about 1010, begins with Gayumars, the first king of the world, who ruled from the mountains, dressed in leopard skins, when men and beasts lived together in peace. In this painting the court gathers in a landscape of rocks that hide faces, among animals, in colours that seem to glow.
It comes from the most splendid Shahnama ever made, with 258 paintings, for the young Shah Tahmasp of Iran, and was counted in its own time the masterpiece of the greatest painter of the age.

hebrew.title: The Great Isaiah Scroll
hebrew.meta: Qumran, about 125 BCE · parchment · Israel Museum, Jerusalem
paras: In 1947 Bedouin shepherds found jars in a cave above the Dead Sea holding scrolls that had lain there for two thousand years. The greatest of them is this: the whole Book of Isaiah, in fifty-four columns of Hebrew on seventeen sheets of parchment sewn together, more than seven metres long.
It is a thousand years older than any copy of Isaiah known before it, and it holds almost word for word the text that has been read ever since: “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people.”

indian.title: Shiva Nataraja, Lord of the Dance
indian.meta: Tamil Nadu, Chola period, about 11th century · bronze · Cleveland Museum of Art
paras: Within a ring of flames Shiva dances the universe into being and out of it again. One hand beats the drum of creation, another holds the fire of destruction, a third is raised to say “do not fear”, and one foot crushes the dwarf of ignorance. His hair flies out with the force of the dance.
The Chola kings had such bronzes carried in procession at the temples where the Tamil saint-poets, the Nayanars, had sung of Shiva dancing in the golden hall of Chidambaram.
indian.credit: Image: Cleveland Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

italian.title: The Map of Hell
italian.meta: Sandro Botticelli, 1480s–90s · ink and colour on parchment · Vatican Library
paras: Botticelli spent years drawing the whole Divine Comedy, a sheet for every canto. This, the only one fully coloured, shows the whole of Dante’s Hell at once: a vast funnel sunk into the earth, ring below ring, from the gate at the top to Satan frozen in the ice at the bottom, with the two poets climbing down through it.
Here is the shape of the Inferno itself: nine circles narrowing as the sins grow worse, every ledge crowded with the damned whom Dante meets and names.

french.title: The Lady and the Unicorn: “À mon seul désir”
french.meta: Paris or Flanders, about 1500 · wool and silk tapestry · Musée de Cluny, Paris
paras: Six tapestries show a lady with a lion and a unicorn on a red ground scattered with flowers and animals. Five stand for the senses; on the sixth she lays a necklace in a casket before a tent inscribed À mon seul désir, “to my only desire”, and no one has ever settled what it means.

They were rediscovered in a château in central France in 1841, and George Sand made them famous. They are the last great image of the courtly love the troubadours sang and the Romance of the Rose allegorised.

nordic.title: The Oseberg Ship
nordic.meta: Norway, built about 820 CE, buried 834 · oak · Museum of the Viking Age, Oslo
paras: In 834 two women of high rank were laid in this ship, with a cart, sledges, beds, animals and treasure, and buried under a mound of earth near the Oslofjord. The clay kept the oak for more than a thousand years, until it was dug out in 1904. Its prow rises into a curling serpent.
It is the funeral the Norse poems know. In the Prose Edda the god Baldr is laid in his ship Hringhorni and burned at sea, and the Eddic poems that tell of the gods were made in this same age.
nordic.credit: Photograph: Larry Lamsa, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

german.title: Walther von der Vogelweide in the Codex Manesse
german.meta: Zürich, about 1300–40 · ink and colour on parchment · Heidelberg University Library
paras: The Codex Manesse gathers the love songs of 140 German poets and paints a portrait of each. Walther, the greatest of them, sits on a rock, legs crossed, chin in hand, his sword beside him and his coat of arms above, lost in thought.
The painter took the pose from Walther’s own poem, “Ich saz ûf eime steine”: “I sat upon a stone, and crossed one leg over the other; on it I set my elbow, and in my hand I laid my chin.”

spanish-portuguese.title: View of Toledo
spanish-portuguese.meta: El Greco, about 1599–1600 · oil on canvas · Metropolitan Museum of Art
paras: A storm breaks over Toledo: the city on its hill, the cathedral and the royal fortress rearranged to suit the painter, the Tagus below, and a sky of thunderous green and grey. It is one of the first great landscapes in Spanish painting.
Toledo was the city of Garcilaso de la Vega, who brought the sonnet into Spanish, and El Greco painted it in the age of Góngora, Lope de Vega and St John of the Cross.
spanish-portuguese.credit: Image: Metropolitan Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

chinese-japanese.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
chinese-japanese.meta: Katsushika Hokusai, about 1830–32 · colour woodblock print
paras: A huge wave curls like a claw over three boats of rowers, and far off, small and still, stands Mount Fuji. It is the first of Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and perhaps the most famous image Japan has made.
Fuji had been sung in Japanese poetry since the eighth century, and a few years later Hokusai began to illustrate the Hundred Poems by a Hundred Poets, the anthology every Japanese child learned.

celtic.title: The Chi Rho Page of the Book of Kells
celtic.meta: Iona or Kells, about 800 · ink and colour on vellum · Trinity College Dublin
paras: The first letters of Christ’s name in Greek, Chi and Rho, fill a whole page in spirals, knots and interlace so fine they can hardly be followed. Hidden among them are angels, an otter with a fish, cats watching mice, and moths.
In this same age an Irish monk wrote, in a book of his own, a poem on his white cat Pangur Bán, who hunts mice while he hunts meanings: one of the first lyrics of the Irish tradition.

russian-slavic.title: The Trinity
russian-slavic.meta: Andrei Rublev, about 1411–27 · tempera on wood · Moscow
paras: Three angels sit at Abraham’s table under the oak of Mamre, heads inclined to one another round a single cup, in a circle of blue, gold and green. Rublev painted it for the monastery of St Sergius, and it has been called the greatest of all Russian icons.
It belongs to the world of the Lay of Igor’s Campaign and of the long Orthodox tradition that Pushkin, Tyutchev and Akhmatova still wrote from.

hungarian.title: The Holy Crown of Hungary
hungarian.meta: 11th–12th century · gold, enamel and pearls · Hungarian Parliament, Budapest
paras: The crown with which the kings of Hungary were crowned for centuries joins a Byzantine band of enamelled saints to a Latin cross-band, topped by the famous bent cross. It was carried abroad in 1945, kept by the United States at Fort Knox, and given back to Hungary in 1978.
For Hungarian poets it is the nation itself: Petőfi’s National Song of 1848, “Rise, Magyar”, and every patriotic poem after it, are written in its shadow.
hungarian.credit: Photograph: CSvBibra, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
